chapters.name: Ozone Layer, Refrigerant Types, and Substitutes
chapters.summary: How chlorine in CFCs and HCFCs harms the ozone layer, how to tell CFC, HCFC, and HFC refrigerants apart, ozone depletion and global warming potential, and substitute refrigerants, oils, and blends.
keyPoints: Chlorine is the part of CFCs and HCFCs that destroys ozone.
CFCs have the highest ozone depletion potential, then HCFCs; HFCs have zero.

chapters.name: Clean Air Act and Section 608 Rules
chapters.summary: The Montreal Protocol, phaseout dates, the venting prohibition, the refrigerant sales restriction, technician certification types, reclaimed refrigerant, recordkeeping, and penalties.
keyPoints: Knowingly venting CFC, HCFC, or HFC refrigerant during service or disposal is illegal.
Recovered refrigerant sold to a new owner must be reclaimed by an EPA-certified reclaimer.

chapters.name: Refrigeration Cycle, Gauges, and the Three Rs
chapters.summary: Refrigerant states and pressures around the cycle, manifold gauge colors, psig and psia, recover, recycle, and reclaim, recovery speed, leak checking, and dehydration evacuation.
keyPoints: Refrigerant absorbs heat in the evaporator and gives off heat in the condenser.
Blue gauge and hose = low side; red = high side; yellow = center hose.

chapters.name: Safety, Cylinders, and Shipping
chapters.summary: Health risks of refrigerant, personal protective equipment, recovery and disposable cylinders, the 80 percent fill limit, using nitrogen safely, and shipping labels.
keyPoints: Never fill a recovery cylinder more than 80 percent full of liquid.
Pressurize for leak tests with nitrogen through a regulator, never oxygen or compressed air.

chapters.name: Small Appliance Recovery Rules
chapters.summary: What counts as a small appliance, the 80 and 90 percent recovery requirements, the 4-inch vacuum option, certified recovery equipment, Type I test formats, and safe disposal by the final processor.
keyPoints: Small appliance = factory-sealed with 5 pounds of refrigerant or less.
Newer equipment and a working compressor: recover 90 percent; otherwise 80 percent.

chapters.name: Small Appliance Recovery Techniques and Safety
chapters.summary: Self-contained and system-dependent (passive) recovery, access valves, recovering from appliances with working and non-working compressors, identifying refrigerant, and decomposition and flammability hazards.
keyPoints: Compressor not working with passive recovery: install access valves on both the high and low sides.
Remove solderless piercing valves when service is finished.

chapters.name: High-Pressure Leak Detection and Leak Repair
chapters.summary: Signs of leaks, leak test gases, leak rate triggers for large appliances, repair deadlines, verification tests, leak inspections, retrofit or retirement plans, and leak repair records.
keyPoints: Trigger leak rates: 20% commercial, 30% industrial process, 10% comfort cooling and others.
Repair within 30 days (120 days if an industrial process shutdown is needed).

chapters.name: High-Pressure Recovery Requirements and Techniques
chapters.summary: Required evacuation levels by appliance type, size, and recovery equipment date, major and non-major repairs, leaky appliances, the 15-pound limit for system-dependent equipment, and ways to speed recovery.
keyPoints: High-pressure under 200 lb with newer equipment: 0 inches Hg; 200 lb or more: 10 inches Hg.
Recover liquid first to speed up recovery.

chapters.name: High-Pressure Systems, Refrigerants, and Safety
chapters.summary: System components and the refrigerant state in each, identifying refrigerants, pressure classes, gauge and absolute pressure, retrofits, and safety around compressors and machinery rooms.
keyPoints: R-22 and R-410A are high-pressure refrigerants.
Never energize a hermetic compressor while the system is under a deep vacuum.

chapters.name: Low-Pressure Leak Detection and Leak Repair
chapters.summary: Why air and moisture leak into low-pressure chillers, signs such as frequent purging, how to pressurize for a leak test, the 10 psig limit, leak rate triggers, inspections, and chronic leak reports.
keyPoints: Leaks in a low-pressure system let air and moisture in.
Do not pressurize a low-pressure chiller above 10 psig for a leak test.

chapters.name: Low-Pressure Recovery, Evacuation, and Recharging
chapters.summary: The 25 mm Hg absolute evacuation level, recovering liquid and then vapor, keeping water moving in the tubes, heating oil before draining, pressurizing for non-major repairs, and charging vapor before liquid.
keyPoints: Low-pressure appliances must be evacuated to 25 mm Hg absolute.
When recharging, add vapor first so water in the tubes does not freeze.

chapters.name: Low-Pressure Chillers, Purge Units, and Safety
chapters.summary: How low-pressure chillers work, the purge unit, the rupture disc, low-pressure refrigerants such as R-123 and R-11, and machinery room safety.
keyPoints: The purge unit removes air and moisture that collect at the top of the condenser.
R-123 machinery rooms need a refrigerant sensor under ASHRAE Standard 15.
